question: What is Redis, where does it keep its data, and what kinds of application problems is it meant to solve?
model_answer: Redis is a server (a TCP daemon) that exposes abstract data types such as strings, lists, sets, hashes and sorted sets under binary-safe keys, and is positioned as a cache, data structure server and document/vector query engine. The data set lives primarily in the computer's memory, which is what gives it low and predictable latency; disk is used only optionally for persistence. Typical uses named by the project are caching, session storage, queues and message brokering (lists, streams, pub/sub), leaderboards and counters, and real-time analytics.
required_facts: Redis is a network server that manipulates abstract data types (strings, lists, sets, hashes, sorted sets, ...) stored under keys
The data set is held primarily in memory, which is the source of its speed and predictable performance
Main use cases include caching, session storage, messaging/queues and real-time analytics

answers.A: Redis is an in-memory data structure server: a network daemon whose commands (such as SET and GET) manipulate typed values in a key space. It keeps its data in RAM as ready-made data structures, with disk storage optional and secondary. It is meant for shared state that many programs must reach with very low (often sub-millisecond) delay: a cache in front of a slower primary database, a session store, a message broker (lists, streams, pub/sub), counters, queues, leaderboards and rate limiters, and search and vector workloads. Its audience is developers of real-time, data-driven applications.
answers.B: Redis is an in-memory key-value store and data structure server: a network server that maps binary-safe string keys to typed values such as strings, lists, sets, hashes and sorted sets. It keeps the dataset primarily in RAM; writing it to disk through RDB snapshots or the append only file is optional. It targets real-time applications where a disk database is too slow for the request path, answering reads and writes often in under a millisecond. Named uses are caching (with eviction and key expiration), session storage, queues and messaging (job queues on lists, priority queues on sorted sets, pub/sub, streams), and secondary indexing, full-text search and vector similarity search.
answers.C: Redis is an in-memory data structure server written in C, shipped as one server binary. It keeps typed values in RAM under string keys, executes commands against them on a single main thread, and can optionally persist and replicate the result. Which application problems it is meant to solve: not stated.
answers.D: Redis is a server program (a TCP daemon) that keeps a key space of abstract data types and lets applications read and change it by sending commands over a network connection. The data set is held primarily in the computer's memory; writes can optionally also be copied to files on disk and to other Redis servers called replicas. It is aimed at developers building real-time data-driven applications, with stated uses of caching, session management, querying/sorting/analytics, messaging and interservice communication, and vector operations. Its data types serve uses such as counters, stacks and queues, leaderboards, rate limiters and event logs.
answers.E: Redis is an in-memory key-value store and data structure server: a single redis-server process runs as a TCP daemon, holds the dataset primarily in RAM, and answers commands such as SET and GET. Disk is an optional extra, used for persistence (RDB snapshots or an append-only file) so the dataset can be reloaded at restart. It targets real-time, data-driven applications that need hot data faster than a disk-backed database: caching (with eviction and key/hash-field expiration), distributed session storage, counters, queues, leaderboards and rate limiters, event store and message broker (lists, sorted sets, sets, streams, pub/sub), and search, query and vector storage for documents and GenAI workloads.
answers.F: Redis is an in-memory data structure server written in C: a TCP daemon whose commands manipulate a key space where keys are binary-safe strings and values are abstract data types such as strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets and streams. The dataset is kept primarily in memory; disk is used only for persistence (snapshots and the append-only file), not as the primary store. It targets developers building real-time data-driven applications, with listed uses of caching, distributed session store, data structure server (counters, queues, leaderboards, rate limiters), NoSQL data store, search and query engine, event store and message broker, vector store for GenAI, and real-time analytics.

question: Redis has two ways of persisting data to disk. What is each one for, how do they differ in durability, and which one is used to restore data at startup when both are enabled?
model_answer: Snapshotting (RDB) periodically dumps the whole dataset to disk when configured save points are met (a number of seconds elapsed together with a number of writes), so a crash can lose the minutes of writes since the last snapshot. The append-only file (AOF) logs the write operations applied to the dataset and gives much better durability: with the default once-per-second fsync at most about one second of writes is lost on power failure. Both can be enabled together, and if AOF is enabled at startup Redis loads the AOF because it has the better durability guarantees.
required_facts: RDB snapshotting saves the whole dataset when a save point (elapsed seconds plus number of changes) is reached, and can lose minutes of writes
AOF is an append-only log of writes with better durability (about one second of loss with the default fsync policy)
Both can be enabled at once; at startup the AOF is loaded in preference to the RDB file

answers.A: An RDB snapshot is a file holding the whole dataset at one moment, written by a forked child when a configured time and number of changes have passed. The append-only file is a log of the write commands applied to the dataset and gives much better durability. With default snapshots a crash or power outage can lose a few minutes of writes depending on the save points, while the append-only file with the default everysec policy loses at most about one second, and with always it syncs after every write. The two can run together, and on restart the append-only file is loaded when it is enabled because it has the stronger guarantee.
answers.B: An RDB snapshot is a point-in-time dump of the whole dataset, written by a forked child when configured save points (enough changes and seconds) are reached; a process problem or power outage can lose a few minutes of writes, depending on the save points. The append only file is a log of every write command, replayed at startup to rebuild the dataset, and gives better durability; how often it is synced is set by appendfsync, and with everysec roughly one second of writes can be lost. When both are enabled, the append only file is loaded at startup because it has the better durability guarantees.
answers.C: RDB is a point-in-time snapshot of the dataset written by a forked child process. AOF is a log of write commands, kept as a set of files described by a manifest: one BASE snapshot, one or more INCR files, and HISTORY files awaiting deletion. How the two differ in durability: not stated. Which one is used to restore data at startup when both are enabled: not stated; the only related fact is that a preload-file option loads a backup, plain RDB or AOF at startup in place of the normal data files.
answers.D: The RDB snapshot dumps the whole data set to a file, written by a forked background child when a save point (seconds elapsed and number of changes) is met or BGSAVE is issued. The Append Only File is an alternative mode that logs each write command. With snapshots alone a process failure or power outage may lose a few minutes of writes, depending on the save points; with the AOF at its default fsync policy (every second) about one second of writes can be lost on a power outage, or a single write if only the Redis process fails. Both can be on at once and each can be off. At startup the AOF is loaded when it is enabled, otherwise the snapshot is loaded; a preload-file setting overrides both.
answers.E: RDB is a binary snapshot of the whole dataset written to disk at configured save points by a forked child, so the parent keeps serving; a crash between snapshots can lose a few minutes of writes. The AOF is a log of every write command that is replayed on restart; with the default everysec fsync policy about one second of writes can be lost, 'always' fsyncs after every write (slowest, safest), and 'no' leaves flushing to the OS. The two are independent and can run together. When both are enabled, the AOF is loaded at startup because it has the better durability guarantees.
answers.F: One form is the RDB snapshot: a point-in-time copy of the dataset written by rdbSave, normally in a forked child when a configured save point (enough changes in enough seconds) is reached, while the parent keeps serving clients. The other is the append-only file (AOF), a log of write commands tracked by a manifest as a BASE file, INCR files of later writes and HISTORY files after a rewrite; it is off by default and its fsync policy (no, always, everysec; default everysec) trades durability against write latency. The two can be enabled together. How much data each can lose is not stated. Which one is used to restore data at startup when both are enabled is not stated; only that start-up loads the AOF manifest and then calls loadDataFromDisk.

question: What is the background I/O service for, what kinds of work does it take off the main thread, and what ordering guarantee does it give?
model_answer: The background I/O service exists so that operations that could block the server are performed on side threads instead of the main thread. It handles three kinds of work: closing files (where the close may actually unlink a file and be slow), fsync of the append-only file, and lazy freeing of memory. Each job type is assigned to one specific worker thread with its own queue, and a worker processes its jobs sequentially in the order they were inserted.
required_facts: It moves slow, potentially blocking operations off the main thread onto background worker threads
The job kinds are background file close, AOF fsync, and lazy freeing of memory
Each job type is bound to one worker, and jobs on a worker are processed in FIFO order

answers.A: Background threads take memory freeing off the main thread: UNLINK and the ASYNC flush options free memory on another thread so a large deletion does not stall every client. What else the background I/O service handles, how it is organised, and what ordering guarantee it gives are not stated.
answers.B: Not stated. A background I/O service, the work it takes off the main thread, and any ordering guarantee are not described. The only related facts given are that optional I/O threads read, parse and write sockets, and that background saves run in a forked child.
answers.C: The background I/O service is a set of worker threads in src/bio.c that take slow work off the main thread, which must never block. The work it takes is closing files, AOF fsync and lazy freeing of memory. What ordering guarantee it gives: not stated.
answers.D: The background job service in src/bio.c uses worker threads to take work off the main thread. The work it does is background close(2) calls, AOF fsync, and lazy freeing of memory. What ordering guarantee it gives is not stated.
answers.E: Not stated. The only related fact given is that UNLINK and the ASYNC option of FLUSHALL and FLUSHDB free memory on another thread so that a large deletion does not block the main thread. The service itself, the full set of work it takes over and any ordering guarantee are not stated.
answers.F: Not stated as a named service. What is supported: an fsync of the append-only file can run in a background thread under the everysec policy, and large objects above a threshold (LAZYFREE_THRESHOLD) are freed in the background by freeObjAsync so that deletes do not stall the main thread. The full list of work types and any ordering guarantee are not stated.

question: What is the modules system for, how is a module brought into a running server, and how does a module's own data type get saved and restored given that the core does not understand it?
model_answer: Modules let Redis be extended beyond its built-in data structures: a module is a shared library that implements new commands (and possibly new data types). It is loaded at startup with a loadmodule directive naming the library and optional arguments, and the server aborts if a module cannot be loaded; the module's load entry point initialises the API and registers each command with flags and key positions. A module-owned value is stored as a special object type whose value is managed only by the module, with a table of function pointers for serialising, deserialising, AOF-rewriting and freeing it, and in the RDB file it is tagged with a 64-bit module type ID so loading is dispatched to the right module.
required_facts: Modules extend Redis with new commands and data types beyond the built-in ones
They are loaded via loadmodule directives at startup (the server aborts if loading fails), and the module's load function registers its commands
Module values are a special object type handled through module-supplied callbacks (serialise, deserialise, AOF rewrite, free)
In RDB a module value carries a 64-bit module type ID used to dispatch loading to the owning module

answers.A: Modules extend the server in-process: a module is a shared library that adds commands and data types through a C modules API, and JSON, search and time series ship this way. A module is loaded into redis-server at runtime through loadmodule lines in the configuration file (redis-full.conf for the bundled ones); bundled modules are pinned in modules/modules.yaml and built against this Redis. How a module's own data type is saved and restored is not stated.
answers.B: The modules API lets developers add new commands and data types beyond the built-in ones. A module is a shared library loaded into redis-server, for example with a loadmodule line in the configuration, so it is loaded at startup; loading into an already running server by command is not stated. How a module's own data type is saved and restored is not stated.
answers.C: Modules extend the server through a public API declared in src/redismodule.h, which modules compile against; JSON, Search, Time Series and the probabilistic types are delivered this way from separate repositories, and vector sets is an in-tree module. Modules are loaded during startup, after cluster initialisation and before listeners open, via loadmodule lines in the configuration (the full configuration file with those lines is generated, not hand-edited). Whether a module can be loaded into an already running server by command: not stated. A module value's encoding is owned by the module, and modules can use key metadata slots 1 to 7; how a module's data type is saved and restored: not stated.
answers.D: Modules extend Redis beyond its built-in data structures and let new commands be implemented quickly; a module is a shared library loaded into redis-server at runtime. It is named with a loadmodule line in the configuration, which is queued by queueLoadModule at startup and then loaded when main calls moduleLoadFromQueue (outside Sentinel mode). External modules are pinned in modules/modules.yaml, fetched with make modules-update and built by make, while vector sets are an in-tree module. How a module registers its commands, and how a module's own data type is saved and restored, is not stated.
answers.E: The modules API lets developers extend the core with new commands beyond the built-in data structures; search, JSON, time series and probabilistic types are bundled as external modules pinned in modules/modules.yaml, while vector sets are kept in-tree. Modules are loaded at runtime through loadmodule lines in the configuration file (a git checkout uses a generated redis-full.conf that carries them); the MODULE command is blocked by default unless enable-module-command allows the caller. How a module's own data type is saved and restored is not stated.
answers.F: The modules API lets Redis functionality be extended beyond the built-in data structures and new commands be implemented quickly; JSON, time series, the probabilistic types and the Query Engine are bundled external modules. Those modules are pinned in modules/modules.yaml, cloned under modules/<name>/src/ by make modules-update, and loaded through the generated redis-full.conf; at start-up main loads modules after initServer and before opening listeners. How a module is loaded into an already running server is not stated. How a module's own data type is saved and restored is not stated.

question: How do the event loop, the connection layer and the client-handling code fit together to make the server run? Describe what one turn of the main loop does.
model_answer: The server is driven by a single event loop that multiplexes file (socket) events and time events over the best polling facility the OS offers (evport, epoll, kqueue, or select as fallback). At initialisation the server registers a periodic timer callback (the server cron), a before-sleep hook, and accept handlers on its listeners; each accepted client gets a read handler installed on its connection, and connections are an abstraction with pluggable types (TCP, Unix socket, TLS). Each turn of the loop runs the before-sleep hook, blocks in the poll call until a descriptor is ready or the next timer is due, runs the after-sleep hook, dispatches the fired read/write handlers, and finally runs due time events.
required_facts: A single event loop handles both file (socket) events and time events, choosing one OS polling backend (evport/epoll/kqueue/select) at build time
Server init registers the periodic cron timer, a before-sleep hook and accept handlers; each client connection gets a read handler
One iteration: before-sleep hook, poll (sleeping until an fd fires or the next timer), after-sleep hook, fired file handlers, then time events
Connections are abstracted behind a connection-type interface (TCP, Unix, TLS)

answers.A: The event loop is a small event-driven library in ae.c; main ends by handing control to its aeMain loop, which drives the whole server. When the listening socket becomes readable, the socket accept handler accepts the connection and creates a client record, and createClient registers readQueryFromClient as that connection's read handler so the loop calls it whenever bytes arrive. That handler fills the client's query buffer, parses complete commands and runs them through processCommand and call, with replies queued on a pending-write list rather than written at once. Before the loop sleeps, beforeSleep flushes the append-only file buffer and then writes the pending replies directly, installing a write handler only when a socket cannot take the whole reply. Any other work done in one turn (for example timers) is not stated.
answers.B: The event loop, built on the library in ae.c, sleeps until file descriptors are ready and then processes their events; aeMain repeats this until the loop is stopped. The listening socket's handler connSocketAcceptHandler accepts a TCP connection and passes it to acceptCommonHandler, which creates a client; createClient installs readQueryFromClient as the read handler, so the loop calls it when bytes arrive. That handler fills the query buffer and processInputBuffer parses and dispatches commands, whose replies go into the client output buffer. Before the loop waits again, beforeSleep flushes the append only file buffer to disk and then calls handleClientsWithPendingWrites to send buffered replies. serverCron periodically checks save points. A fuller per-turn ordering (timers, other before/after-sleep work) is not stated.
answers.C: The main thread runs one event loop from src/ae.c, with one OS backend compiled in (epoll, kqueue, evport or select). Before each poll, beforeSleep() handles pending TLS and decompressed data, cluster and slot-migration housekeeping, blocked clients, a fast expire cycle, the AOF flush, pending client writes, hand-off to I/O threads and asynchronous client frees, then releases the modules GIL. After the poll, afterSleep() reacquires the GIL first; when a connection is readable, readQueryFromClient() in src/networking.c reads into the client's query buffer, the input is parsed into commands, executed, and replies go to the client's output buffer to be written from beforeSleep() or by an I/O thread. A timer, serverCron(), runs at a rate set by hz for client timeouts, database maintenance (expiry, rehashing, defrag), replication cron and persistence triggers. Connection types are initialised at startup, but how the connection layer itself is structured: not stated.
answers.D: The event loop in src/ae.c is aeMain, which repeatedly calls aeProcessEvents; each turn runs beforeSleep, waits in aeApiPoll for ready sockets, runs afterSleep, then runs the file (socket) events and time events. On the connection side, connSocketAcceptHandler accepts a socket and hands it to acceptCommonHandler, which rejects it at maxclients or calls createClient, which installs readQueryFromClient as the read handler. When a socket is readable the loop calls that handler, which reads into the query buffer, parses it in processInputBuffer and dispatches to processCommand. The time event runs serverCron (server.hz times per second) for active expiry, rehashing, starting saves and replication reconnection. beforeSleep flushes the AOF and then sends buffered replies through handleClientsWithPendingWrites and writeToClient; a ready socket normally fires its read handler before its write handler, and AE_BARRIER inverts that. How the connection layer abstracts different transports is not stated.
answers.E: main initialises the server and listeners, loads saved data, then enters aeMain, which repeatedly calls aeProcessEvents in src/ae.c. Each turn sleeps until a file (socket) event fires or a timer is due, then runs the registered handlers. For a new TCP connection the accept handler in src/socket.c accepts the socket and hands it on to createClient in src/networking.c, which registers readQueryFromClient as that connection's read handler; later bytes are read into the client's query buffer, parsed, and passed to processCommand and call in src/server.c. Replies are appended to the client's output buffer and the client is put on a pending-write queue rather than installing a write handler. Just before the loop sleeps again, beforeSleep flushes the AOF buffer and then sends the pending replies.
answers.F: The event loop library (src/ae.c) picks the best available multiplexing backend and aeMain repeatedly calls aeProcessEvents; main sets up the server, opens listeners, loads data and then enters that loop. When a listening socket is readable, the socket accept handler accepts a bounded number of new connections per cycle and hands each to acceptCommonHandler, which creates a client and registers readQueryFromClient as the connection's read handler. On a readable client, bytes are read into the query buffer, parsed (multibulk if the buffer starts with '*', inline otherwise) and each complete command is passed to processCommand and then call. Replies are appended to the client's output buffer and the client is put on a pending-write queue. Before each wait, the beforeSleep hook runs: it writes pending reply buffers to sockets, and the accumulated append-only-file buffer is written out just before the loop is entered again.

question: How is a database's keyspace organised in memory: what containers hold keys and their expirations, how does that layout change in cluster mode, and where is a key's name stored relative to its value?
model_answer: Each database holds a main keyspace store, a second store indexing the keys that have a timeout, and a third structure for sub-key expirations (currently hash fields), plus bookkeeping tables for blocked and watched keys. The stores are 'kvstores': an array of hash tables rather than a single one. In standalone mode there is one hash table; in cluster mode there is one per hash slot (2^14 of them, allocated on demand), so all keys of a slot can be reached easily. The key name is not a separate object: the key (and optional metadata such as the expiry, and small string values) is embedded in the same allocation as the value object.
required_facts: A database has a main keys store plus a separate store for keys with an expiration (and one for sub-key/hash-field expirations)
Each store is an array of hash tables: one table in standalone mode, one per hash slot in cluster mode
The key string (and optional expiry metadata) is embedded in the same allocation as the value object

answers.A: Not stated. Only that a server holds a key space of key-value pairs in memory, with keys being binary-safe strings and values abstract data types; the containers for keys and expirations, the cluster-mode layout and where a key's name is stored relative to its value are not stated.
answers.B: Not stated beyond the basics: a server holds a keyspace in memory in which each key is a binary-safe string naming one value, and in cluster mode keys are divided over 16384 hash slots by the CRC16 of the key. The containers that hold keys and expirations, how that layout changes in cluster mode, and where the key name is stored relative to its value are not stated.
answers.C: Each database holds two kvstore instances, keys and expires; a kvstore is an array of dicts. In cluster mode there is one dict per hash slot (16,384); otherwise there is one dict. A Fenwick tree over the dict sizes makes finding the Nth key and the next non-empty slot cheap. A third structure, subexpires, tracks hashes that have fields with a TTL, keyed by their earliest field expiry. The key name is embedded directly after the stored object's struct (a small string value may be embedded too), and the key's expiry time sits in metadata slot 0 placed before the struct.
answers.D: Not stated. The only supported facts are that keys are binary-safe strings naming values, and that a value is an object holding its type, encoding, LRU or LFU data, a refcount and a pointer to the payload; the containers for keys and expirations, the cluster-mode layout and where the key name sits relative to the value are not stated.
answers.E: Not stated. It is only stated that every command acts on one keyspace whose keys are binary-safe strings and whose values are one of several data types, and that cluster mode divides the keyspace into 16384 hash slots. The containers holding keys and expirations, how that layout changes in cluster mode, and where a key's name is stored relative to its value are not stated.
answers.F: Not stated.

question: A stored value has both a 'type' and an 'encoding'. What is the difference, why do both exist, and who decides which encoding a value uses?
model_answer: The type is the logical data type the user sees (string, list, set, sorted set, hash, stream, module value, ...), while the encoding says which in-memory representation currently implements it. Several types have multiple encodings optimised for memory footprint or speed: for example compact listpack or integer-set forms for small collections versus hash tables and skiplists for large ones, and integer or embedded forms for short strings. The generic object code only chooses encodings for strings; for the other types, the code implementing each type's commands picks and converts the encoding as the value grows. A sorted set in its full form, for instance, keeps the same elements in both a hash table (element to score) and a skiplist (ordered by score).
required_facts: Type is the logical data type; encoding is the current in-memory representation of that value
One type can have several encodings, trading memory footprint against speed (compact forms for small values, hash table/skiplist forms for large)
String encodings are chosen in the generic object code; other types' encodings are managed by the code implementing that type's commands

answers.A: Not stated. A value has one data type (string, list, set, hash, sorted set, stream and so on), each with its own commands and time and space costs; encodings, why both exist and who chooses an encoding are not stated.
answers.B: Not stated. A data type is described only as the kind of value a key holds (string, list, set, hash, sorted set); encodings, why both exist, and who chooses the encoding are not described.
answers.C: A value object carries a type, an encoding, a reference count and a pointer. The type is the kind of value (string, list, set, sorted set, hash, stream, array, module); the encoding is the in-memory representation used for it, for example listpack or hash table for a set. Both exist because a type usually has a compact encoding for small values and a general one for larger ones. The switch is governed by thresholds set in redis.conf; for module types the encoding is owned by the module. Beyond those thresholds, who decides the encoding of a given value: not stated.
answers.D: The type is what a value is: an abstract data type such as a string, list, set or hash, defined by its operations and their complexity. The encoding is how that value is represented in memory at the moment, recorded in the object's encoding field; strings may be RAW, EMBSTR or INT, sets may be INTSET or HT, lists use a quicklist (a linked list of listpacks) and streams a radix tree of listpacks. Both exist so that small values can use memory-saving compact representations under the same type. A value stays in its compact form until it passes configured limits such as hash-max-listpack-entries, hash-max-listpack-value, set-max-intset-entries, set-max-listpack-entries and zset-max-listpack-entries. Which piece of code makes the choice is not stated.
answers.E: Not stated. The only related fact is that 8.10 added compact hashes, described as a hash encoding that stores field names once for keys sharing a schema to reduce memory use. The general distinction between type and encoding, why both exist and who chooses the encoding are not stated.
answers.F: Not stated.

question: How is the clustering code divided, and how does a cluster node decide which hash slot a key belongs to and whether it should serve the command or redirect the client?
model_answer: The clustering code is split into a common part shared by any clustering implementation (key-space handling, slot computation, deciding which node serves a query) and a separate part implementing the standard cluster-bus based mechanism. A key maps to one of 16384 slots by taking the low 14 bits of the CRC16 of the key; if the key contains a non-empty {...} section only that part is hashed, so related keys can be forced into the same slot. For each command with keys the node works out the owning node: if it is itself the command runs, otherwise the client gets a MOVED or ASK redirection, and commands whose keys fall in different slots are refused.
required_facts: Cluster code is split into a generic/common part and a part specific to the cluster-bus (gossip) implementation
There are 16384 slots; slot = CRC16(key) reduced to 14 bits
If the key contains a non-empty {...} hash tag only the tagged part is hashed
Commands for slots owned elsewhere are redirected (MOVED/ASK); keys spanning different slots are rejected

answers.A: A cluster divides keys into 16384 hash slots; a key's slot is computed by keyHashSlot from the CRC16 of the key, or of the part inside braces if the key has one, so braces can force keys into the same slot. The slot computation lives in cluster.h and slot routing in cluster.c; how the clustering code is otherwise divided is not stated. A command whose keys span more than one slot is rejected with a cross-slot error. How a node decides between serving a command and redirecting the client is not stated.
answers.B: A key belongs to one of 16384 hash slots, given by the CRC16 of the key name; the mapping is defined in src/cluster.h. During command checking, processCommand redirects the client when the key is owned by another cluster node, and otherwise the command proceeds; multi-key operations work only when all keys share a slot. Cluster nodes talk to each other on a separate bus port. How the clustering code is divided into files or layers is not stated.
answers.C: src/cluster.c holds the parts common to any clustering implementation: slot calculation, redirection decisions and generic CLUSTER subcommands. src/cluster_legacy.c is the standard gossip-based cluster bus: node table, failure detection, failover and config epochs; atomic slot migration and per-slot statistics are separate files. A key's slot is the CRC16 of the key, or of the text inside {...} if present, masked to 14 bits. The redirection check runs in the command gate after command lookup, arity, authentication and ACL checks, and is driven partly by the command's key specs. The rule by which a node decides to serve or redirect: not stated.
answers.D: Cluster code lives in src/cluster.c and src/cluster_legacy.c (with slot migration in src/cluster_asm.c); cluster.c covers routing and redirection, and the code as a whole maps keys to slots, routes requests and handles node failure, but exactly which responsibilities sit in which file is not stated. keyHashSlot takes the crc16 of the key and keeps its low 14 bits, giving one of 16384 slots; if the key has a {...} part only that part is hashed, so related keys can share a slot. processCommand calls getNodeByQuery, which returns the node serving that slot: if it is this node the command runs here, otherwise clusterRedirectClient replies with a MOVED error, or ASK during a migration, giving the slot and the node's address. Keys in different slots get -CROSSSLOT and a multi-key request during a slot migration can get -TRYAGAIN.
answers.E: How the clustering code is divided into files is not stated. A key's hash slot is the low 14 bits of the CRC16 of the key, giving 16384 slots; if the key contains a part inside { and }, only that part is hashed, so related keys can be forced into the same slot. In processCommand, when cluster mode is enabled, getNodeByQuery finds which node owns the command's keys; if it is another node, clusterRedirectClient redirects the client there. A command whose keys fall in different slots gets a cross-slot error before it runs.

A key's slot is one of 16384, computed as the low 14 bits of the CRC16 of the key, or of only the part between '{' and '}' when present, so related keys can share a node. During command processing, processCommand uses getNodeByQuery to find the node serving the key's slot and, if that is another node, redirects the client with clusterRedirectClient instead of executing the command.

question: Walk through what happens to a write command from the moment its bytes arrive on a client socket until it has been executed and made durable or replicated. What checks can stop it before execution?
model_answer: The connection's read handler reads bytes into the client's query buffer and the input-buffer processor parses complete commands into an argument vector. The command processor then looks the command up in the command table and rejects unknown names or wrong arity, checks authentication and ACL permissions, performs cluster redirection if the keys belong to another node, tries to evict data if memory is over the limit (rejecting with an out-of-memory error if it cannot), and refuses writes when persistence is failing, when too few replicas are connected, or when the node is a read-only replica. If the client is inside a transaction the command is queued instead; otherwise the core call routine executes it and, if it changed the dataset, propagates it to the AOF buffer and to the replication stream. The AOF buffer is written to disk in the before-sleep hook, before replies are delivered to clients.
required_facts: Bytes are read into a per-client query buffer and parsed into arguments before the command is looked up in the command table (unknown command / wrong arity rejected)
Pre-execution checks include authentication/ACL, cluster redirection, maxmemory eviction (OOM rejection), and write refusals (disk error, not enough replicas, read-only replica)
Inside MULTI the command is queued instead of executed
After execution a data-modifying command is propagated to the AOF buffer and to replicas; the AOF buffer is flushed before returning to the event loop / replying

Otherwise call runs the command's implementation, notices the dataset changed and records the command for propagation; when the outermost execution unit ends the recorded commands are propagated (several wrapped in MULTI/EXEC), appended to the AOF buffer by feedAppendOnlyFile and to the replication stream by replicationFeedSlaves. The reply is queued on the pending-write list, and before the loop sleeps beforeSleep flushes the AOF and only then writes replies, so a client is never told about a write the log does not hold. Writes are also refused by default after a failed background save with save points configured, and a master can be configured to stop accepting writes when too few replicas are connected.

Inside MULTI the command is queued and answered QUEUED; otherwise call runs the command's proc function, which writes its reply with addReply into the output buffer. After a write, call hands the command to alsoPropagate, and propagateNow feeds it to feedAppendOnlyFile (a memory buffer) and replicationFeedSlaves (the replication stream). In beforeSleep, flushAppendOnlyFile writes the buffer to disk before handleClientsWithPendingWrites sends the replies; fsync frequency follows appendfsync.

The AOF is flushed before the event loop's next poll, with fsync done by a background thread, and the reply is written from the same pre-poll step or by an I/O thread.
answers.D: The event loop calls readQueryFromClient when the socket is readable; it reads bytes into the query buffer and processInputBuffer parses them (input starting with * as multibulk, otherwise inline) into a pending command; an I/O thread may read and parse but must queue the client for the main thread. processCommand looks the command up and can refuse it for: authentication required, ACL denial (-NOPERM), cluster routing to another node (redirect), failed eviction for a deny-on-memory-limit command (OOM error), a disk persistence error, a write on a read-only replica, or the server still loading data. Otherwise call runs the command's handler (setCommand for SET, which stores the key, raises server.dirty and queues the OK reply). Because dirty changed, the command is queued with alsoPropagate and sent to both feedAppendOnlyFile (into the AOF buffer) and replicationFeedSlaves when the outermost unit finishes, with several commands from one unit wrapped in MULTI/EXEC. Just before the loop sleeps, beforeSleep flushes the AOF buffer to the file first, then sends the buffered reply to the client.
answers.E: The event loop fires the client's read handler, readQueryFromClient, which reads the bytes into the client's query buffer; processInputBuffer chooses inline or multibulk parsing, and on an I/O thread it only flags and queues the client for the main thread. processCommand then looks the command up and can stop it for: unknown command or wrong argument count, ACL denial, a cluster redirect to another node (or cross-slot error), an out-of-memory rejection when eviction fails for a command flagged as denied on OOM, a disk-error block on writes after a failed save or AOF write, and DEBUG/MODULE being disabled; a client pause postpones the client rather than rejecting it, and inside MULTI the command is queued and answered QUEUED. Otherwise call runs the command's handler, which answers via addReply into the output buffer and pending-write queue. For a write, call schedules propagation with alsoPropagate, and afterwards propagatePendingCommands calls propagateNow, which appends to the AOF buffer if AOF is on and feeds the replicas (several commands from one execution unit are normally wrapped in MULTI/EXEC). Before the loop sleeps, beforeSleep writes the AOF buffer to the file and only then sends replies, so the write reaches the log before the client hears OK; replication is asynchronous and the master does not wait for replicas.
answers.F: readQueryFromClient reads the bytes into the client's query buffer and processInputBuffer parses them (multibulk when the buffer starts with '*', otherwise inline); with I/O threads the parsing may happen off the main thread, and the client is then flagged and queued to the main thread, which alone executes commands. processCommand looks the command up in the command table, checks ACL permissions, in cluster mode redirects the client if another node serves the key's slot, runs eviction when maxmemory is set and rejects deny-OOM commands with an OOM error if eviction fails, rejects writes with MISCONF after a failed snapshot when stop-writes-on-bgsave-error is set, and rejects writes with NOREPLICAS when min-replicas-to-write is not met. Inside MULTI the command is only queued and the client gets QUEUED. question: How does a background rewrite of the append-only file work, step by step, and how does the server keep track of which files make up the log while writes continue?
model_answer: The append-only log is a set of files tracked by a manifest: at most one base file (a snapshot as of the last rewrite), one or more incremental files holding the writes since then, and history files left over from earlier generations. On a rewrite the parent first flushes its buffer and opens a new incremental file to keep logging, then forks; the child writes a fresh snapshot of the dataset to a temporary file and exits. When the parent sees the child succeeded, it renames the temporary file to a new base file name, marks the previous base and the already-covered incremental files as history, persists the updated manifest, and deletes the history files in a background thread.

The parent opens a new incremental file and forks; the child writes a new snapshot to a temporary file
On success the parent renames the temp file to the new base, marks the old base and old incremental files as history, and persists the manifest
History files are deleted afterwards in the background

What is stated is that since Redis 7 the append only file is a set of files: a base snapshot, incremental command files, and a manifest that orders them. Writes are appended to a memory buffer and flushed to disk before the event loop sleeps.

A rewrite is done by a forked child and produces a new BASE. The manifest is what records which files make up the log. After a rewrite the old BASE and INCR files become HISTORY files, which are removed automatically unless garbage collection is disabled. The base file uses the RDB format by default. The detailed steps of the rewrite between the fork and the manifest update are not stated.

The log is rewritten in the background with BGREWRITEAOF, triggered automatically when it grows by auto-aof-rewrite-percentage. question: When a replica connects (or reconnects) to a master, how does the master decide between sending only the missing data and doing a full resynchronization, and what happens in each case?
model_answer: The replica asks to continue from a given replication ID and offset. The master accepts a partial resynchronization only if that ID matches its current replication ID (or its secondary ID, up to the offset where that history ended) and the requested offset is still inside its replication backlog, an in-memory buffer of recent replication stream; it then replies that it can continue and sends the backlog from that offset onward. Otherwise it falls back to a full resynchronization: it tells the replica the new replication ID and offset, produces an RDB snapshot in a forked child (written to disk and then transferred, or streamed directly to replica sockets in diskless mode), and the replica loads it. A bigger backlog lets replicas survive longer disconnections without a full resync.
required_facts: The replica presents a replication ID and offset; the master compares the ID with its own (current or secondary) replication IDs
Partial resync also requires the requested offset to still be covered by the replication backlog buffer; then only the missing backlog portion is sent
Otherwise a full resync happens: the master announces a new ID/offset and transfers an RDB snapshot produced by a child process (via disk or directly over the socket)

answers.A: After a short disconnect a replica catches up from the master's replication backlog instead of receiving a full copy. When a full copy is needed it is by default streamed straight to the replica sockets (diskless sync), which works better with slow disks and fast networks. How the master decides between the two cases is not stated.
answers.B: A replica connects with SYNC or PSYNC, handled by syncCommand. The master keeps a replication backlog, a buffer of recent writes; after a short disconnect the replica can resume from that backlog with a partial resync and receive only what it missed, instead of copying everything again. Otherwise a full resynchronization is done. The exact conditions the master tests (such as IDs or offsets) and the steps of a full resynchronization are not stated.
answers.C: A replica first attempts a partial resynchronization (PSYNC) served from the primary's replication backlog; if that fails, a full sync is done by transferring an RDB. The exact criteria the master uses to accept or refuse the partial resync: not stated. In a full sync using the RDB channel, the replica opens a second connection so the forked child streams the RDB directly while the main connection carries live writes, which the replica buffers until loading finishes; this moves buffering pressure from primary to replica. What happens step by step in the partial case beyond using the backlog: not stated.
answers.D: The replica connects (replicationCron sees the connect state and calls connectWithMaster, with syncWithMaster as handler) and sends PSYNC with a replication ID and offset. On the master, syncCommand calls masterTryPartialResynchronization, which accepts when the replication ID matches and the requested offset is still inside the replication backlog; it then answers +CONTINUE and the replica gets only the part it missed. Otherwise the master answers +FULLRESYNC, runs startBgsaveForReplication to produce an RDB, and the replica receives that RDB in readSyncBulkPayload. In both cases the master afterwards streams write commands through replicationFeedSlaves, and a replica passes its master's stream unchanged to its own replicas.
answers.E: A replica is configured with replicaof <masterip> <masterport> and reconnects by itself after a network partition; it resynchronizes partially when the link was lost only briefly, otherwise fully. A full sync sends an RDB file, either written to disk first or, by default (repl-diskless-sync yes), streamed by a child straight to the replica sockets; because a replica arriving after the transfer starts must wait for the next one, the master waits repl-diskless-sync-delay seconds (5 by default) to gather replicas. How the master decides between partial and full resynchronization, and the handshake and what is sent in the partial case, are not stated.
answers.F: Not stated. Only the entry points on the master are identified, syncCommand and startBgsaveForReplication; how the choice between partial and full resynchronization is made and what happens in each case is not stated.

question: How do keys with a time-to-live actually get removed? Describe the mechanisms involved, how the background one limits its own cost, and how removal is kept consistent on replicas and in the append-only file.
model_answer: Expired keys are reclaimed in two ways: lazily, when a key is accessed and found to be past its expiry, and actively, by a background cycle that samples keys with timeouts so that keys never accessed again are still freed. The active cycle is adaptive and runs in two forms: a slow cycle from the periodic server timer (hz times per second) bounded to a percentage of CPU time, and a short fast cycle run before each sleep of the event loop, bounded to about a millisecond; it stops working on a database once the estimated fraction of expired keys is low. Only the master deletes: when it removes an expired key it sends an explicit delete to replicas and the AOF, while replicas do not delete expired keys themselves but report them as expired to readers until the master's delete arrives.
required_facts: Two mechanisms: lazy expiration on access and an active background expire cycle
The active cycle has a slow form run from the periodic timer and a fast form run before sleeping, each with a time limit, and is adaptive to how many keys are expired
The master propagates a delete (DEL/UNLINK) for each expired key to replicas and the AOF
Replicas do not delete expired keys on their own; they wait for the master's delete while still treating the key as logically expired for reads

How the background cycle limits its own cost is not stated. How expiry is kept consistent on replicas and in the append-only file is not stated (it is only stated that replicas receive DEL commands for keys the master evicts).

question: Why does eviction pick victims using an approximation instead of tracking exact least-recently-used order, how does the approximation work, and what does that choice cost?
model_answer: Exact LRU ordering would need extra memory per key, so Redis uses an approximation that runs in constant memory: each object carries only a small access clock (or frequency counter), and when a key must be evicted the server samples a handful of keys (five by default) and feeds the best candidates into a small fixed-size pool kept across eviction calls, then evicts the best entry in the pool. The cost is accuracy: the evicted key is not guaranteed to be the globally oldest one. The sample size is tunable to trade CPU for accuracy (ten samples comes very close to true LRU but costs more CPU, three is faster but less accurate).

It samples a small number of keys (default 5) and keeps the best candidates in a small fixed-size pool across calls, evicting the best one
The trade-off is accuracy versus CPU, tunable via the sample size (more samples = closer to true LRU but more CPU)

question: Why are the main hash tables resized incrementally rather than all at once, and why is resizing discouraged while a background save or rewrite child is running? What does each choice cost?
model_answer: Rehashing is spread over many small steps (one bucket at a time, piggybacked on ordinary lookups and updates, plus about one millisecond of active rehashing ten times a second) so that growing a huge table never blocks the single main thread for a long time; the cost is that two tables coexist and use extra memory until rehashing finishes, and active rehashing can add occasional small delays. While a forked child is saving, resizing is avoided because the child shares memory pages with the parent copy-on-write, and moving lots of entries would cause many pages to be copied. The cost of that is that tables may run denser than ideal during a save; resizing is only forced when the load factor exceeds a hard ratio, and inside the child itself it is forbidden entirely.

The cost of incremental rehashing is extra memory while two tables coexist (and small latency from active rehashing)
With a child process active, resizing is avoided to limit copy-on-write page copying
Resizing is still allowed when the fill ratio passes a forced threshold (elements/buckets of 4 or more)

question: Why does Redis execute commands on essentially one thread, where does it nevertheless use extra threads, and what are the stated costs or conditions of doing so?
model_answer: The project's stated philosophy is that threading is not a silver bullet: an efficient, mostly single-threaded core is simpler, and scaling is achieved by running several such shared-nothing instances combined by higher-level features like Redis Cluster, which also keeps each instance's dataset small enough for persist-by-fork to work well. Parallelism was only considered worthwhile for I/O, the low-hanging fruit. Accordingly, optional I/O threads handle client socket reads, protocol parsing and writes while command execution stays on the main thread (I/O threads hand clients back to the main thread and never free clients themselves), and other side threads handle things like lazy freeing and slow file operations. I/O threading is off by default and recommended only on machines with at least four cores, leaving a spare core, and only when CPU is actually the bottleneck.
required_facts: The core is deliberately (mostly) single-threaded for simplicity; scaling comes from multiple shared-nothing instances (e.g. Redis Cluster)
Extra threads are used only for I/O (socket reads, parsing, writes) and background chores such as lazy freeing; command execution stays on the main thread
I/O threads are disabled by default and advised only with 4+ cores and a real CPU bottleneck
