question: What trade-off do the append-only file's sync policies offer, why is the log written just before the event loop sleeps rather than inside each command, and what durability is given up while a background save is running if the related mitigation is turned on?
model_answer: There are three fsync policies: never (let the OS flush when it wants: fastest, least safe), every write (slow, safest) and once per second (the default compromise). Because a client must not get a reply before its write is in the log, and replies can only go out when the event loop is re-entered, all AOF writes of an iteration are accumulated in a memory buffer and written just before sleeping; with the always policy a write barrier ensures a socket is not read and replied to in the same iteration before that flush. Since fsync can block for a long time while a child is doing heavy disk I/O, an option lets the server skip fsync during a background save or rewrite, which reduces latency but means durability is temporarily the same as the never policy (up to about 30 seconds of log could be lost with default Linux settings).
required_facts: Three policies: no fsync (fastest), always (safest, slow), every second (default compromise)
AOF writes are buffered and flushed just before re-entering the event loop so the log is written before the client is answered
Skipping fsync during a background save/rewrite trades durability (equivalent to no fsync, up to ~30 s of loss) for lower latency

answers.A: The sync policies trade speed for durability: no lets the operating system flush when it chooses and is fastest, always fsyncs after every write and is slowest and safest, and the default everysec fsyncs once a second and can lose about one second of writes in a power outage. Commands are appended to an in-memory buffer and the buffer is written just before the event loop sleeps because a reply can only leave on a later pass of the loop, so the log is written before any reply goes out. With no-appendfsync-on-rewrite set to yes, fsync is skipped while a background save or rewrite is busy to avoid stalling the main thread, and up to 30 seconds of log can be lost with default Linux settings.
answers.B: appendfsync sets how often the log is fsynced, trading durability against disk I/O; everysec fsyncs once per second as a compromise and can lose about one second of writes. The other policy values are not stated. Writes are appended to a memory buffer and flushAppendOnlyFile writes it to disk in beforeSleep, before replies are sent, because the log must be written before replying to the client. What durability is given up during a background save when the related mitigation is turned on is not stated.
answers.C: The append-only file is flushed in the step that runs before each event-loop poll, and fsync is done by a background thread. What trade-off the sync policies offer: not stated. Why the log is written before the loop sleeps rather than inside each command: not stated. What durability is given up during a background save with the mitigation turned on: not stated.
answers.D: The appendfsync policy trades speed for safety: no never fsyncs and lets the OS flush (fastest), always fsyncs after every write (slow, safest), and everysec, the default, fsyncs once per second as a compromise that can lose about one second of writes. Commands append to an in-memory AOF buffer, and the buffer is written by flushAppendOnlyFile from beforeSleep, ahead of sending replies, so that with always the write reaches the file before the reply goes out. With always, a failed write makes the process exit because the reply may already be buffered and the change cannot be rolled back. With no-appendfsync-on-rewrite set to yes, up to 30 seconds of log can be lost in the worst case with default Linux settings.
answers.E: The sync policies trade speed for durability: 'no' never fsyncs and lets the OS flush when it wants (fastest), 'always' fsyncs after every write to the log (slow, safest), and 'everysec' fsyncs once per second (the default compromise, can lose about one second of writes in a power outage). Commands only append to an in-memory AOF buffer; the buffer is written just before the event loop sleeps and before replies are sent, so a client is told OK only after its write is in the file. With no-appendfsync-on-rewrite yes, long fsync stalls while a child is saving are avoided, but during that time durability drops to that of appendfsync no, which can mean up to 30 seconds of lost log with default Linux settings.
answers.F: The sync policies (no, always, everysec; default everysec) trade durability against write latency; how much data each can lose is not stated. The log is accumulated in a memory buffer and written just before the event loop is entered again because it must be written before replying to the client, and the client socket can only be written when the event loop is entered. Under everysec the flush may be delayed while an fsync is still running in the background thread, since on Linux the write would be blocked by it anyway. The durability given up during a background save when the related mitigation is turned on is not stated.

question: If you wanted to add a new built-in command, where is the command table defined, how does it get into the running server, and what besides the handler function must you describe about the command?
model_answer: Commands are declared as one JSON description per command in a commands folder under the source directory; a generator script in the utilities folder reads all of them, links subcommands to their container commands, validates key specifications, and writes a generated definitions file that must not be edited by hand. That generated file is included by the command-table source to form a static table, and at startup the server walks the table and inserts each command (and its subcommands) into its command dictionary, plus a second dictionary unaffected by renames. Besides the handler function, the description carries arity, command flags (write, read-only, fast, allowed while loading, etc., which also drive ACL categories), group, and key specifications.
required_facts: Each command is described in a JSON file in the commands folder of the source tree
A generator script turns those JSON files into a generated definitions file (not hand-edited) that is compiled into the static command table
At startup the static table is loaded into the server's command lookup dictionary
The description includes metadata such as arity, flags, group and key specs, not just the handler

answers.A: Not stated where the command table is defined or how it is loaded into the running server. Only that processCommand finds a command by name with lookupCommand, rejects wrong argument counts, and runs the implementation through the command's proc function pointer; what else must be described about a command is not stated.
answers.B: Not stated. It is only stated that processCommand looks up the command and that call runs the command's proc function; where the command table is defined, how it is loaded into the server, and what metadata a command must declare are not described. The only extension route described is the modules API, which adds commands through a loaded shared library.
answers.C: Each command is described by a JSON file under src/commands/, from which utils/generate-command-code.py generates src/commands.def; src/commands.c includes that generated file, which is how the table gets compiled into the server. The handler is a function of the form void nameCommand(client *c) in the relevant source file. Besides the handler, the description must give the command's name, arity, flags (such as write, denyoom, fast) and key specs. Those flags drive the command gate, ACLs and cluster routing, so they are part of correctness.
answers.D: Commands are defined as JSON files under src/commands (for example set.json and get.json). utils/generate-command-code.py reads those JSON files and generates commands.def, which src/commands.c includes with COMMAND_STRUCT set to redisCommand; at run time processCommand finds a command with lookupCommand and call invokes its handler through the command's proc pointer. Commands carry properties such as being marked deny-on-memory-limit and whether they need authentication, but the full list of what must be described besides the handler is not stated.
answers.E: Not stated for the most part. It is stated only that processCommand resolves commands with lookupCommand and rejects wrong argument counts, that call invokes the command's handler through c->cmd->proc (e.g. setCommand and getCommand in src/t_string.c), that commands carry flags such as the one denying them when out of memory, and that src/commands/README.md describes generated command metadata. Where the command table is defined, how it gets into the running server, and the full description a command needs are not stated.
answers.F: The command table is built in src/commands.c, which includes the generated file commands.def to form the redisCommand table; there is also a src/commands/ directory with its own README. At runtime the server resolves a client's argument vector against server.commands with lookupCommand, and execution calls the entry's proc function. Commands carry flags, for example a deny-OOM flag that makes the command rejected when memory cannot be freed. What else must be described about a new command, and how commands.def is generated, is not stated.

question: Where would you add a new configuration parameter, and what determines whether it can be changed at runtime, what its default is, and whether changing it triggers any action?
model_answer: Configuration parameters are rows in one static table in the configuration source file. Each row is created with a type-specific constructor (boolean, integer, enum, string, ...) that binds a user-visible name and optional alias to the server field that stores the value, with a default, bounds or validity function, and an optional apply callback run after a runtime change. A flag on the row says whether the parameter is modifiable at runtime or immutable (runtime set attempts on immutable ones are refused, and protected ones need extra permission). The same row serves startup loading, runtime get/set and rewriting of the config file; the user-facing explanation belongs in the commented sample configuration file.
required_facts: All standard parameters live in a single static table of typed entries in the configuration source file
Each entry binds a name to a server variable with a default (and bounds/validator) and an optional apply function called on runtime change
A per-entry flag marks it modifiable or immutable; immutable ones cannot be set at runtime

answers.A: Not stated.
answers.B: Not stated. Configuration is described only through settings in redis.conf (for example appendfsync, maxmemory-policy, loadmodule); where a parameter is defined in code, and what governs runtime mutability, defaults or change actions, are not described.
answers.C: A new parameter is one line in the static_configs[] table in src/config.c, written with a create*Config macro, plus a field in struct redisServer and a documented entry in redis.conf. Flags such as IMMUTABLE_CONFIG and MODIFIABLE_CONFIG decide whether CONFIG SET can change it at runtime. What determines its default: not stated. Whether and how changing it triggers an action: not stated.
answers.D: Configuration handling, including compiled defaults (for example maxmemory 0 and io-threads 1) and the loadmodule queueing, lives in src/config.c, and the shipped redis.conf documents each setting. Some sensitive directives are immutable and governed by enable-protected-configs, and settings can be changed on a live server through the CONFIG command. Where exactly a new parameter is declared, and what determines its runtime mutability, its default and any action triggered on change, is not stated.
answers.E: Not stated. The only related facts are that directives controlling the files Redis writes, such as dir and dbfilename, are immutable at runtime, and that enable-protected-configs defaults to no. Where a new parameter is added and what determines its runtime mutability, default and any triggered action are not stated.
answers.F: Configuration parameters and their defaults are registered in src/config.c (for example appendonly off, appendfsync everysec, maxmemory-policy noeviction, io-threads 1). What determines whether a parameter can be changed at runtime, and whether changing it triggers an action, is not stated.

question: Where is it decided when a small hash, set, sorted set or list stops using its compact representation, and how would you tune or change that behaviour?
model_answer: The switch points are configuration thresholds documented in the advanced section of the sample configuration: for hashes, sets and sorted sets a maximum number of entries and a maximum size of the biggest entry for the compact listpack form (sets of integers have their own integer-set entry limit), and for lists a maximum size or element count per internal node plus a compression depth. The conversion itself is performed by each type's implementation: for example the hash code checks, when fields are written, whether the number of fields or the length of a value exceeds the thresholds and converts the listpack to a real hash table. So tuning is a configuration change, while changing the conversion rules means editing the type's own source file.
required_facts: Thresholds are configuration directives: max entries and max entry size for the compact form of hashes, sets and sorted sets (plus an integer-set limit for sets and a per-node size for lists)
The conversion is carried out in each data type's own implementation when a write exceeds the threshold (e.g. hash converts listpack to hash table)
Default limits: hashes 512 entries / 64-byte values; sets and sorted sets 128 entries / 64 bytes

answers.A: Not stated.
answers.B: Not stated. Compact representations of small hashes, sets, sorted sets or lists, and the thresholds for leaving them, are not described.
answers.C: Each type has a compact encoding for small values and a general one, and the thresholds between them are settings in redis.conf, so tuning means changing those settings. The type's own file (t_hash.c, t_set.c, t_zset.c, t_list.c) implements its encodings. For hashes, automatic conversion to the template encoding is controlled by hash-min-template-entries, which is 0 (off) by default and one-way. The exact function where the conversion decision is made, and the names of the other thresholds: not stated.
answers.D: The switch away from the compact form is governed by configuration limits: hash-max-listpack-entries and hash-max-listpack-value for hashes, set-max-intset-entries and set-max-listpack-entries for sets, and zset-max-listpack-entries for sorted sets; a value stays compact until it passes them. Tuning is done by changing those settings in the configuration. Where in the code the conversion decision is made is not stated, and no threshold for lists is stated (lists are a linked list of listpacks).
answers.E: Not stated.
answers.F: Not stated.

question: Where would you plug in (a) support for a different operating-system readiness-notification API and (b) a new kind of client transport alongside TCP, Unix sockets and TLS?
model_answer: The polling backend is selected at compile time inside the event-loop library: it includes exactly one backend implementation file, tried in order of expected performance (evport, epoll, kqueue, then select), so a new OS API means a new backend file plus a new branch in that selection. A transport is added by implementing the connection-type interface (a table of callbacks for init, configure, accept, read/write handlers, address lookup and so on) and registering it with the connection-type registry, which holds a small fixed number of types keyed by name. TCP and Unix types are mandatory at startup, while TLS registration may fail when the server is built without TLS support.
required_facts: The OS polling backend is a compile-time choice inside the event-loop library, one implementation file per API, ordered by performance
A transport is an implementation of the connection-type callback interface registered by name in a registry
TCP and Unix socket types are required; TLS is optional and depends on a build flag

answers.A: Not stated. Only that the event loop library is in ae.c and the TCP accept handler is in socket.c; where to add another readiness-notification API or a new transport is not stated.
answers.B: Not stated. The event loop is built on the library in ae.c and connections are accepted by connSocketAcceptHandler and handed to acceptCommonHandler, with TLS optional via BUILD_TLS=yes, but where a new readiness-notification backend or a new transport type would be plugged in is not described.
answers.C: (a) The event library in src/ae.c compiles in one backend from ae_epoll.c, ae_kqueue.c, ae_evport.c or ae_select.c, so a new readiness API would be another backend file of that kind. (b) Connection types are initialised during startup, before the configuration is parsed; where a new transport is defined or registered: not stated.
answers.D: (a) The event loop in src/ae.c selects its multiplexing layer from separate backend files, trying ae_evport.c, then ae_epoll.c, then ae_kqueue.c, and falling back to ae_select.c, so a new readiness API would be another such backend chosen in src/ae.c. (b) The TCP accept path is connSocketAcceptHandler in src/socket.c, which hands sockets to acceptCommonHandler, and TLS can be built in or built as a module; where a new transport type is registered is not stated.
answers.E: Not stated for both parts. (a) The event loop lives in src/ae.c, but how an operating-system readiness-notification API is plugged in is not stated. (b) The TCP accept handler lives in src/socket.c and TLS can be built into the server or as a loadable module, but the extension point for a new transport is not stated.
answers.F: (a) The readiness-notification backends are selected in the event loop library, src/ae.c, which includes the best available of evport, epoll, kqueue or select; a new backend would sit alongside those, though the exact interface it must implement is not stated. (b) The TCP accept handler lives in src/socket.c, and TLS can be built in or built as a loadable module; how a new transport type is defined and registered is not stated.

question: What happens when the configured memory limit is reached, in which situations will writes start failing, and what memory or which instances are not subject to the limit in the way you might expect?
model_answer: When memory use exceeds the limit, Redis tries before executing commands to evict keys according to the selected policy, for a bounded time per call so the server stays responsive (continuing in a timer if needed). If the policy is no-eviction (the default) or no suitable key exists (for example a volatile policy with no keys that have a TTL), commands that would use more memory are rejected with an error while reads keep working. Replica output buffers and AOF buffers are deliberately not counted as used memory, to avoid a feedback loop where eviction deletes fill the buffers and trigger more eviction; so real memory can exceed the limit and headroom should be left. Replicas by default ignore the limit entirely and just follow the master's deletes, so they can use more memory than configured.
required_facts: On reaching the limit, keys are evicted per the configured policy; eviction work is time-bounded per call
With the no-eviction policy (the default) or when nothing is evictable, memory-increasing write commands get an error while reads continue
Replica output buffers and AOF buffers are excluded from the counted memory to avoid an eviction feedback loop
Replicas ignore maxmemory by default and may exceed it

answers.A: The maxmemory cap is enforced before each command by performEvictions, which frees memory by evicting keys according to the policy. With the noeviction policy, or when no key fits the policy, write commands fail while reads still work. Which memory or which instances are not subject to the limit is not stated.
answers.B: When memory use reaches maxmemory, keys are evicted according to maxmemory-policy; processCommand runs eviction before executing a command. Under the default policy, noeviction, writes return errors, and in general when no key can be evicted, write commands that need memory get errors. Which memory or which instances are exempt from the limit is not stated.
answers.C: A maxmemory eviction step runs in the command gate before a command executes, preceded by a separate client-memory eviction step, and a command's denyoom flag is among the flags that drive that gate. Exactly what happens when the limit is reached, in which situations writes fail, and which memory or instances are not subject to the limit: not stated.
answers.D: When maxmemory is set, processCommand calls performEvictions before running a command, which frees keys according to maxmemory-policy. If memory cannot be freed (the default policy is noeviction, or no key qualifies), commands marked deny-on-memory-limit get an OOM error while read-only commands such as GET keep working. Replica output buffers are outside what the limit protects: with replicas attached it is suggested to set a lower maxmemory to leave free RAM for them (not needed under noeviction), and a forked child adds copy-on-write memory pressure. The compiled default is 0 (commented out in the shipped file), and a 32-bit instance with no limit is given a 3 GB maxmemory with noeviction at startup. Whether any kind of instance ignores the limit is not stated.
answers.E: When maxmemory is set, processCommand runs performEvictions before a command; eviction removes keys under the configured policy, working for a bounded time and continuing later from a timer so a large overshoot does not freeze the server. The default policy is noeviction; whenever nothing can be evicted, commands that would use more memory are refused with an out-of-memory error while reads still work. The output buffers feeding attached replicas are not counted toward the limit (to avoid a loop of evictions filling them with DEL commands and triggering more evictions), so a lower maxmemory is suggested to leave room. Replicas ignore maxmemory by default and instead receive DEL commands for keys the master evicts, so they can use more memory than the limit.
answers.F: When maxmemory is set, eviction (performEvictions) runs before a command executes if the server is over the limit; it samples candidate keys into a pool and evicts for a bounded period so the server stays responsive. If nothing more can be evicted it returns a failure, and commands flagged deny-OOM, the writes that would grow memory, are rejected with the error "OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'", while reads continue. The default policy is noeviction, so with defaults such writes fail as soon as the limit is exceeded. Which memory is excluded from the limit and which instances are exempt is not stated.

question: How does the server behave when persistence goes wrong: when a background snapshot fails, when the append-only file is damaged at startup, and when the data file cannot be loaded at all?
model_answer: If snapshots are enabled and the latest background save failed, the server by default stops accepting write commands (so the operator notices), and accepts them again once a background save succeeds; AOF write or fsync errors likewise cause writes to be denied. At startup, an AOF that is merely truncated at the end is by default loaded as far as possible with a log message, but if that option is off the server refuses to start, and an AOF corrupted in the middle always makes the server exit with an error (unless a small corrupt tail is explicitly allowed to be cut off). A fatal error loading the RDB file, or a failed AOF load, makes the server exit rather than start with partial data.
required_facts: After a failed background save (with save points configured) writes are refused by default until a save succeeds; AOF write/fsync errors also block writes
A truncated AOF tail is loaded as much as possible by default; with that option disabled the server refuses to start
Corruption in the middle of the AOF, or a fatal RDB load error, makes the server exit at startup

answers.A: If a background save fails while save points are configured, the server by default stops accepting writes until saving works again, so the persistence problem cannot go unnoticed. What happens when the append-only file is damaged at startup, and when the data file cannot be loaded at all, is not stated.
answers.B: If a background save fails, the server by default stops accepting writes so that the failure is noticed; processCommand refuses writes after a persistence error. Behaviour when the append only file is damaged at startup and when the data file cannot be loaded at all is not stated.
answers.C: The command gate includes a disk-error write refusal, so writes can be refused when there is a disk error. What specifically happens when a background snapshot fails, when the append-only file is damaged at startup, or when the data file cannot be loaded: not stated.
answers.D: After a failed background save, stop-writes-on-bgsave-error makes the server refuse writes, so the user learns the hard way that data is not persisting; the command gate checks this through writeCommandsDeniedByDiskError and returns a disk error message. With appendfsync always, a failed AOF write makes the process exit. When a preload-file backup manifest is configured, startup aborts if the target is missing or cannot be loaded. What happens when the append-only file is damaged at startup, or when the normal data file cannot be loaded, is not stated.
answers.E: If a background snapshot fails, stop-writes-on-bgsave-error yes makes the server refuse writes until saving works again, so a broken disk is noticed rather than silently losing data; write commands are likewise blocked after a failed AOF write. RDB files end with a CRC64 checksum that makes the format more resistant to corruption at roughly a 10% cost when saving and loading, and it can be disabled. What the server does when the append-only file is damaged at startup, and when the data file cannot be loaded at all, is not stated.
answers.F: If the fork for a background snapshot fails, the parent records the failure. If snapshotting has failed and stop-writes-on-bgsave-error is set, commands that may modify the dataset are refused with a MISCONF error until the condition clears; this is checked in processCommand through writeCommandsDeniedByDiskError. What happens when the append-only file is damaged at startup is not stated. What happens when the data file cannot be loaded at all is not stated.

question: What consistency and durability guarantees does master-replica replication NOT give, what can an operator configure to narrow the exposure, and how does a replica behave towards clients when its link to the master is down?
model_answer: Replication is asynchronous, so a write acknowledged by the master may not have reached any replica and can be lost on failover. A master can be configured to stop accepting writes unless at least N replicas are connected with a lag of at most M seconds, but this explicitly does not guarantee that N replicas received a given write; it only bounds the window of exposure. A replica that has lost its master, or is still synchronising, by default keeps answering queries with possibly stale or even empty data; it can instead be configured to return an error for data commands. Replicas are read-only by default, and loading a sync payload directly from the socket without first storing it on disk carries its own data-loss risks if the transfer fails.
required_facts: Replication is asynchronous, so acknowledged writes can be lost
A minimum-replicas / maximum-lag setting can make the master refuse writes, but it does not guarantee the write reached that many replicas, it only limits the exposure window
A disconnected or syncing replica serves stale (possibly empty) data by default, or can be set to reply with an error instead

answers.A: Replication is asynchronous, so a replica is not guaranteed to hold every write the master has accepted and may serve out-of-date data. An operator can configure a master to stop accepting writes if it appears not to be connected to at least a given number of replicas. By default a replica that has lost its master keeps answering clients, possibly with stale data, because replica-serve-stale-data is yes; its behaviour with that setting turned off is not stated.
answers.B: Replication is asynchronous, so acknowledged writes can be lost on failover. A master can be configured to stop accepting writes if it appears not to be connected to at least a given number of replicas; this does not guarantee that N replicas will accept a write, it only limits the window of exposure for lost writes to the specified number of seconds. How a replica behaves towards clients while its link to the master is down is not stated.
answers.C: Which consistency and durability guarantees replication does not give: not stated. A min-replicas write refusal exists in the command gate, so an operator can have writes refused under a min-replicas condition; its exact semantics are not stated. The command gate also has read-only replica and stale replica checks, so a replica can refuse commands on those grounds; the precise behaviour toward clients when the master link is down: not stated.
answers.D: Replication is asynchronous, so replicas lag and acknowledged writes can be lost. A master can be configured to stop accepting writes when it does not appear connected to at least a given number of replicas (min-replicas-to-write); this does not guarantee that N replicas accept a write, it only limits the window of exposure for lost writes to the specified number of seconds. Diskless loading on a replica may cause data loss during failovers because the RDB is not immediately stored on disk, and parsing the RDB from the socket safely needs more memory. A read-only replica rejects writes from normal clients. How a replica treats clients while its link to the master is down is not stated.
answers.E: Replication is asynchronous: the master streams each propagated write to replicas and does not wait for them, so it gives no guarantee that a write has reached a replica when it is acknowledged; a replica with a broken link may hold stale data. An operator can set min-replicas-to-write (off by default) so the master stops accepting writes when fewer than a given number of replicas appear connected. While its link to the master is down, a replica by default still answers reads with possibly stale data (replica-serve-stale-data yes) and by default rejects writes (replica-read-only yes).
answers.F: Replication is asynchronous, so a write acknowledged by the master is not guaranteed to have reached a replica; how much acknowledged data a failover can lose is not stated. The one guard an operator can configure is min-replicas-to-write, under which the master rejects writes with NOREPLICAS when not enough good replicas are connected. How a replica behaves towards clients while its link to the master is down is not stated.

question: What restrictions does running in cluster mode impose on commands and databases compared with a standalone server, and what happens to the cluster's availability when some hash slots have no serving node?
model_answer: In cluster mode a command may only address a single key or several keys that all hash to the same slot, and multi-key commands are additionally refused while that slot is being migrated; commands whose keys span slots fail with a cross-slot error, which follows from the project's position that multi-key operations cannot be distributed transparently. Only one database is available: the number of databases is forced to 1 and selecting another database is not allowed. By default, if any hash slot is uncovered the whole cluster stops accepting queries until all slots are covered again; this can be relaxed so the covered part keeps serving, and another option allows reads while the cluster is down.
required_facts: Multi-key commands must have all keys in the same hash slot, otherwise they are rejected (and are refused while the slot is unstable/migrating)
Cluster mode has a single database: the database count is forced to 1 and SELECT is not allowed
By default the cluster stops accepting queries if any slot is uncovered; an option lets the covered subset keep serving

answers.A: In a cluster, multi-key commands work only when all their keys are in the same hash slot (braces in key names can force this); a command whose keys span slots is rejected with a cross-slot error. Restrictions on databases are not stated, and what happens to availability when some hash slots have no serving node is not stated.
answers.B: In cluster mode multi-key operations work only when all keys are in the same hash slot, and clients whose keys live on another node are redirected. The cluster bus has no authentication of its own unless TLS is enabled for it. Restrictions on databases and what happens to availability when some slots have no serving node are not stated.
answers.C: In cluster mode the keyspace uses one dict per hash slot (16,384), commands pass a cluster redirection check, and scripts calling into the server have cluster checks applied. What restrictions cluster mode places on commands and databases compared with standalone: not stated. What happens to availability when some hash slots have no serving node: not stated.
answers.D: A node must be started with cluster-enabled yes, since a normal instance cannot join a cluster. A request whose keys fall in different hash slots is rejected with -CROSSSLOT, and a multi-key request during a slot migration can get -TRYAGAIN; commands for slots served elsewhere are redirected with MOVED or ASK. If some hash slots are no longer covered, the whole cluster eventually becomes unavailable, a behaviour the cluster-require-full-coverage option changes. Any restriction on databases in cluster mode is not stated.
answers.E: In cluster mode all keys of one command must map to the same hash slot; a command whose keys fall in different slots gets a cross-slot error before it runs, and a command for keys owned by another node is redirected. Multi-key operations are deliberately not made distributed transparently; a hash tag in braces can force related keys into one slot. Restrictions on databases in cluster mode are not stated. What happens to availability when some hash slots have no serving node is not stated.
answers.F: In cluster mode keys are spread over 16384 hash slots and a node redirects the client when the key's slot is served by another node. Multi-key operations cannot be made transparently distributed across instances; instead keys that must be used together can be forced into the same slot by a shared '{...}' part of the key, and commands exist to migrate keys between instances. Restrictions on databases in cluster mode are not stated. What happens to cluster availability when some slots have no serving node is not stated.
